title: Tannin
content: Tannins are polyphenols extracted from grape skins, seeds, stems and oak. They create a drying, astringent sensation on the gums and cheeks. High-tannin wines (Cabernet Sauvignon, Nebbiolo, Syrah) feel grippy when young and soften with age. Tannin, alongside acidity, is a key preservative that lets red wines age.

title: Acidity
content: Acidity gives wine freshness and makes the mouth water. Cool-climate wines (Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Chablis) are high in acid; warm-climate wines are softer. Acidity balances sweetness and, together with tannin, underpins a wine's ability to age. Low-acid wines taste flabby.

title: Body
content: Body is the perceived weight or fullness of wine on the palate, driven mainly by alcohol and dissolved solids. Light-bodied examples include Pinot Noir and Gamay; full-bodied examples include Napa Cabernet and Barossa Shiraz. Think of the difference between skim milk and cream.

title: Bordeaux Left Bank vs Right Bank
content: On Bordeaux's Left Bank (Medoc, Graves) gravel soils favour Cabernet Sauvignon, giving structured, tannic, cassis-driven blends built to age. On the Right Bank (Saint-Emilion, Pomerol) clay and limestone favour Merlot, giving rounder, plummier, earlier-drinking wines. Both blend in Cabernet Franc.

title: Burgundy and Pinot Noir
content: Red Burgundy is made almost entirely from Pinot Noir, a thin-skinned, terroir-transparent grape giving light-to-medium body, high acidity, red-fruit and earthy notes. White Burgundy is Chardonnay. The region's fame rests on its patchwork of climats where small differences in slope and soil change the wine.

title: Sangiovese and Tuscany
content: Sangiovese is the backbone of Tuscan reds: Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. It shows high acidity, firm tannin, and savoury sour-cherry, tomato-leaf and dried-herb character. It pairs naturally with tomato-based Italian food.

title: Riesling
content: Riesling is an aromatic white grape ranging from bone-dry (Alsace, Clare Valley) to lusciously sweet (German Auslese and beyond). It keeps piercing acidity at all sweetness levels, shows lime, green apple and petrol notes with age, and is one of the longest-lived white wines.

title: Orange (skin-contact) wine
content: Orange wine is white wine fermented with extended skin contact, the way reds are made. This extracts colour, phenolics and tannin, giving an amber hue, a tea-like grip and oxidative, nutty, dried-fruit flavours. It is ancient (Georgian qvevri) yet fashionable in the natural-wine scene.

title: Food pairing basics
content: Match weight to weight and use structure to cut or complement. High-acid wines cut through fat and refresh (Champagne with fried food). Tannic reds soften against protein and fat (Cabernet with steak). Sweetness should meet or exceed the dish's sweetness. Salt tames bitterness and boosts fruit.

title: Champagne and traditional method
content: Champagne gets its bubbles from a second fermentation in the bottle (methode traditionnelle). Time on the dead yeast (lees) adds bready, brioche complexity. Most is a blend of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. Non-vintage is a house-style blend; vintage is a single strong year.

title: Decanting and serving temperature
content: Decant young tannic reds to aerate and soften them, and old reds to separate sediment. Serve whites cool (7-12C) to preserve freshness, reds slightly below room temperature (14-18C); too warm makes alcohol dominate, too cold mutes aroma and hardens tannin.

title: Reading a wine label
content: Old World labels emphasise place (appellation) which implies the grape and style by law; New World labels emphasise grape variety. Look for producer, vintage, region/appellation, alcohol and any quality tier (e.g. DOCG, Grand Cru, Reserva). Place plus vintage often tells you more than the grape alone.

title: Tasting sequence
content: Taste in a fixed order so a sense is not skipped. Look first: color, how deep it is, and whether the rim is watery or stained. Smell the still wine, swirl, then smell again. On the palate, move through sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol, body, flavors, and finish. Only then conclude: which grape or style, which kind of climate, and whether it is ready to drink. Classroom tastings and beginner guides share this order. The words can stay plain.

title: What to look for in the glass
content: Appearance is evidence, not decoration. A purple rim on a red usually means the wine is young; a brick or garnet rim means it has aged. A pale lemon white is often cool-climate; a deep gold white may be riper, older, or oaked. Legs or tears show alcohol and sugar, and they are a weak clue compared with color. Name the color and the intensity before you smell.

title: Aroma families
content: Name the family before the perfect noun. Fresh grass, leaf, or green pepper sits in the herbaceous family, common in Sauvignon Blanc and in Cabernet picked less ripe. Jam, baked berry, or raisin is ripe or dried fruit, not a fresh berry. Vanilla, toast, cedar, and pencil shavings usually come from oak, or from the cedar-and-graphite side of Cabernet. If the family is not in the notes, say so instead of inventing a bottle.

title: Order of checks on the palate
content: On the palate, separate structure from flavor. Sweetness is tasted at the tip and is rare in a dry table wine. Acidity makes the mouth water. Tannin dries the gums and cheeks, mostly in reds and in skin-contact whites. Alcohol feels warm or hot. Body is the weight, from skim milk to cream. Flavors may repeat the nose or change. Check these one at a time so a drying finish is not mistaken for sourness.

title: Finish and length
content: The finish is what remains after you swallow or spit. Length is how long a distinct flavor stays, counted in seconds, not how strong the alcohol burn is. A short finish drops away at once. A long finish keeps a flavor you can name. Bitterness or heat that lingers is not the same as fruit that lingers. Mention length when you judge the wine, and say which flavor lasted.

title: Judging quality without a score
content: A quality judgment is four questions, not a number. Balance: do acid, tannin, alcohol, and fruit sit together, or does one shout. Intensity: how loud the flavor is. Complexity: how many separate things you can name. Length: how long flavor stays after swallowing. A simple wine can still be pleasant. Typicity asks whether it tastes like its grape and place. Give the reason in a sentence before any score.

title: How a bottle review is organized
content: A bottle review is a tasting note with a name attached. It usually states the producer and wine, then appearance, then aroma, then palate, then a short conclusion about style or readiness. The conclusion is the reviewer's judgment of that bottle. It is not a fact about every wine of that grape. Use a review to see how the sequence is written. Do not treat one writer's adjectives as the definition of the grape.
